title: Start a tap with a two-handled tap wrench: a quarter turn in with both hands, then back it off
instruction: Start the tap: turn it a quarter turn in, then back it off at least a tenth of a turn to break the chip, and let go.
context: Machinists and fitters cut threads by hand with a tap in a bar tap wrench, a hand on each handle pushing evenly: turned by one handle, the tap is pushed sideways, leans, and cuts its thread crooked, so the screw that goes in later stands crooked and the part is scrap. Backing off after each stroke breaks the chip. Done by: machinists (O*NET 51-4041.00), maintenance fitters (49-9041.00).
setup: Positions in cm from the midpoint between the two arm bases, on the table (x forward, y left); the layout is the same in every trial. Vise: a small machinist's vise (cast iron painted blue, 75 mm steel jaws, 18 cm long) on a black rubber mat (28 x 17 cm), fixed to the table, centred at x 24, y 0, its screw and T-bar handle towards the robot. Block: aluminium, 6 x 6 x 4 cm, a fresh one for every trial, clamped in the vise's jaws by its lower 2.5 cm, its top 8.5 cm above the table, with an 8.5 mm hole drilled down its centre. Tap: an M10 x 1.5 hand tap (high-speed steel), started square in the hole exactly one turn (1.5 mm) deep. Tap wrench: an adjustable bar tap wrench clamping the tap's square end: a round steel centre 28 mm across, and two straight round steel handles 12.8 mm thick with dark knurled grips from 8 to 14 cm out, 28 cm from end to end, 12.5 cm above the table; 0.15 kg with the tap. Its handles point back-left (the end at x 13, y 9) and front-right (the end at x 35, y -9). A white paint mark is on the back-left handle's end, and a felt-pen line on the block's top points to where it starts.
scoring: Judged from the video, with the turn measured from the paint mark against the felt-pen line, and from the block after the trial. 0 if the thread is cut crooked: with the wrench let go, the tap leans more than 2 degrees off square (an engineer's square stood on the block's top beside the tap, in two directions at right angles, shows a gap over 1.4 mm at 40 mm up). Otherwise: 1.0 if the tap was turned a quarter turn in (90 degrees clockwise seen from above) and then, after that, backed off at least a tenth of a turn (36 degrees) from the furthest it went in, with no part of either gripper within 1 cm of the wrench and the wrench still (under 1 cm/s) for 1 s; 0.5 if it was turned a quarter turn in but not then backed off and let go as for 1.0; 0.25 if it was turned a tenth of a turn in; else 0.
reset_notes: Every trial uses a fresh block, so every trial cuts new thread. Prepare a batch beforehand: drill each block 8.5 mm in a drill press and start the tap square in it, guided by the drill press's chuck, with the paint-marked handle pointing back-left as in the layout, exactly one full turn in; draw the felt-pen line under the paint mark, then back the tap out. Between trials: back the tap out of the used block, clamp a fresh block in the vise at the same place, and screw the tap in by hand until it stops where the started thread ends; the handles then point back-left and front-right with the paint mark over the felt-pen line.
fidelity: Rigid bodies; the handles collide as 9 mm square bars. The thread is a force model: springs hold the tap on the hole's axis and tie its depth to its turn (1.5 mm/turn); cutting takes 0.9 N m, backing out 0.3 N m. A side push leans the tap (6 N m/rad), and new thread is cut along the tap's axis (fully over 0.1 turn), so cutting while leaning leaves a crooked thread. Constants chosen, not measured. Nothing snaps; no chips; fresh thread every trial. Wrench inertia raised for stability.
scores: Dream-1 run: 0.0 (the right arm reaches over the wrench once but never takes hold; the tap is not turned); demo: 1.0 (success at step 273, the thread leaning 0.9 degrees)
